root_idea.summary: A root orientation of turning around and gathering parts together.
root_idea.development: Turning produces winding, wrapping, and circular formation; gathering produces bundling, compacting, and the alternation or overlaying of one thing upon another. Several nominal branches extend this orientation to grouped camels, saddles, bee structures, and regions.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Displayed under the normalized Form II perfect citation form.

senses.definition: To wrap, roll, or fold something together; to gather it into a compact whole.
senses.usage_conditions: In the passive expression إِذَا الشَّمْسُ كُوِّرَتْ (81:1), the sun is described as wrapped or folded up, with its light gathered, removed, or extinguished in the associated explanations.

senses.definition: To cause one thing to pass over, overlay, or encircle another in succession.
senses.usage_conditions: In يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ and its reciprocal construction (39:5), night and day are brought successively upon one another, with their relative increase and decrease.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To wind or wrap a turban around the head; by extension, to wind a thing into a round form.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Form I usage; the Form II derivative is also associated with intensified or repeated winding.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To be in a state of increase or good condition before passing into decrease or defect.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used in the idiom حَارَ بَعْدَ مَا كَارَ; the saying is also interpreted as a return from obedience or a right course.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To carry a bundle or load called كَارَة on one's back.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Form I verbal usage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To collect goods and bind or tie them, or to place them one upon another.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A Classical Form II construction concerning collected or stacked goods.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To throw someone down gathered together or to prostrate him.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The action may follow striking or piercing, but prostration is also reported without an explicitly stated blow.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To fall or fall down, become prostrate, or fall upon one's side while drawing oneself together.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Form V usage; the descriptions of falling, becoming prostrate, and drawing oneself together are grouped as one intransitive branch.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To wrap oneself up and tuck up one's garment or skirt.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Form V reflexive usage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To put on a turban or attire oneself with one.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Form VIII usage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of a horse, to turn or raise its tail while running.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specialized Form VIII usage concerning a horse in motion.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A turn or twist of a turban.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A nominal usage, also used for the individual turns composing a turban.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Increase, abundance, or redundancy.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Occurs in the expression الحَوْرُ بَعْدَ الكَوْرِ, referring to decrease or defect after increase; a variant reading uses الكَوْنِ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A large group or gathered body of camels, reported as approximately one hundred and fifty.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A collective nominal usage explained through the idea of camels gathered together.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A camel's saddle, or a saddle together with its equipment.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The vocalization كُورٌ is distinguished from كَوْرٌ ‘a turn or increase’; variant pronunciations are discussed in the lexical evidence.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A blacksmith's fire-place or clay hearth; according to some, the leather skin used to blow the fire.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The fire-place meaning is primary in the cited explanations; the bellows-skin sense is disputed and is elsewhere assigned to كِيرٌ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A nest or constructed habitation of hornets or bees.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The term can denote the place or structure made by the insects.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A bundle or load carried on the back, especially a tied bundle of clothes or a quantity of wheat.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The lexical descriptions include both a clothes bundle enclosed and tied in one piece of cloth and a carried quantity of grain.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A province, district, tract, or region containing associated towns and villages; also a city or provincial city.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The regional sense is the commonest in the cited usage; the word is also reported as possibly non-Arabic in origin.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A beehive or habitation for bees, including a structure made of clay, twigs, or both.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The term may refer to a constructed bee habitation, including one containing honey.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Honey contained in the beeswax.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A related lexical usage distinct from the hive or bee-habitation sense.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A turban.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A nominal designation; related feminine forms are cross-referenced in the lexical material.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A stranger.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An attributed supplemental usage explicitly applied to a man.

cautions: The interpretations associated with 81:1 range from wrapping or folding the sun to gathering or removing its light; these are retained as variants within the same Quranic wrapping construction.
The historical citation attached to the Lane discussion of the sun is not used to derive the modern verse location; 81:1 is identified independently by QAC.
